summary: Defines semantics for grouping source flows and Forward Error Correction repair flows in SDP, to be used with the SDP Grouping Framework (RFC 5888). It supports additive repair flows and SSRC-level grouping for RTP streams. It is a Proposed Standard and replaced RFC 4756.

plainLanguage.summary: When data is sent with spare copies that can rebuild a lost piece, the spare copies travel in separate streams. This document defines the lines in a session description that say which spare stream belongs to which data stream, and which spare streams may be used together to repair missing data. It replaces an earlier version of those lines that could not say everything without ambiguity.

questions: how to describe fec repair flows in sdp
how to group fec repair flows in sdp
what is an additive repair flow
subtitle: How SDP says which repair streams protect which source streams, including repair streams that are decoded together.

tldr.problem: Forward error correction sends repair packets in separate streams from the source packets, so a receiver must be told which repair stream protects which source stream. The earlier scheme in RFC 4756 could not express every relationship unambiguously.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines the FEC-FR grouping semantics for the SDP group attribute, where each group line is one FEC group and a flow may appear in several groups. It defines the same semantics for ssrc-group when streams share one RTP session.
tldr.outcome: FEC-FR replaces the older FEC semantics, which are deprecated but kept as a fallback for peers that do not understand FEC-FR. The document replaces RFC 4756.

today: RFC 5956 is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 4756. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Repair Flows Need Grouping
sections.content:
Any application that needs a reliable transmission over an unreliable packet network has to cope with packet losses. Forward Error Correction (FEC) is an effective approach, and it is particularly useful in multicast and broadcast applications where feedback from the receiver is potentially limited.

In short, FEC groups source packets into blocks and applies protection to generate a desired number of repair packets. These repair packets may be sent on demand or independently of any receiver feedback; the choice depends on the FEC scheme, the loss characteristics of the underlying network, the transport scheme and the application. At the receiver, lost packets can be recovered by erasure decoding, provided a sufficient number of source and repair packets have been received.

One of the most basic schemes is the parity code, where an exclusive OR (XOR) operation applied to a group of packets, the source block, generates a single repair packet. That scheme gives full recovery if only one packet is lost within the source block and the repair packet is received.

The FEC Framework requires source and repair packets to be carried in different streams, called the source flows and the repair flows. The receiver has to know which flows are which, and the exact association between them, so it can use the correct data to repair the original content after a loss. SDP, through the grouping framework of RFC 5888 and this document, carries that information.
sections.plainLanguage: Some data is sent with spare copies that can rebuild a lost piece. The spare copies travel in separate streams, so the receiver needs a list saying which spare stream belongs to which data stream.

sections.title: Requirements the Grouping Must Meet
sections.content:
The grouping semantics for FEC must be able to indicate four things: that a given source flow is protected by multiple different FEC schemes; that multiple repair flows are associated with a given FEC scheme; that multiple source flows are grouped before FEC protection is applied; and that one or more repair flows protect a group of source flows.

That became possible because RFC 5888 obsoleted RFC 3388, so that a media line, identified by its mid attribute, may appear in more than one a=group line using the same semantics. With that change a sender can indicate the specific associations between source and repair flows, and a receiver can determine which repair flow or flows protect which source flow or flows.

The document also adds support for additive repair flows, which RFC 4756 did not include. Additivity means that multiple repair flows may be decoded jointly to improve the recovery chances of missing packets in a single or the same set of source flows. Additive repair flows can be generated by the same FEC scheme or by different FEC schemes.

Implementations must use the semantics introduced in Sections 4.1 and 4.3. In addition to those requirements, implementations are recommended to support the older FEC semantics for backward compatibility in the scenarios of Section 4.5.
sections.plainLanguage: The list has to cover four cases, including two spare streams that repair the same data and two streams repaired together by one spare stream. This document also allows spare streams to be used together, which the older version did not.

sections.title: The FEC-FR Grouping Semantics
sections.content:
Each a=group line indicates an association relationship between source and repair flows, and the flows included in one line are called an FEC group. If an FEC group contains more than one repair flow, those repair flows must be considered additive. Repair flows that are not additive must be indicated in separate FEC groups. Additivity is not necessarily a transitive relationship, so each set of additive repair flows has to be stated explicitly in the session description.

A source or repair flow may appear in more than one FEC group. Two flows that are additive in one FEC group are not necessarily additive in another.

Using the framework in RFC 5888, the document defines FEC-FR as the grouping semantics that indicates support for the FEC Framework features. The a=group:FEC-FR semantics must be used to associate the source and repair flows, except when the source and repair flows are specified in the same media description, that is the same m line, which is covered in Section 4.3.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line in the list names one set of related streams. Spare streams named on the same line can be used together; spare streams on different lines cannot. A stream can be named on more than one line.

sections.title: An SDP Example
sections.content:
For the scenario in Figure 1, where repair flow R1 protects source flow S1 and repair flow R2 protects the group of S1 and S2, the document writes a=group:FEC-FR S1 R1 and a=group:FEC-FR S1 S2 R2. The flow S1 appears in both groups, which the older FEC semantics could not express. Each flow is in its own media description with a mid attribute naming it, and in the example each flow is carried in its own RTP session.

For additivity, suppose R5 and R6 are additive but R7 is not additive with either. The session description then reads a=group:FEC-FR S4 R5 R6 and a=group:FEC-FR S4 R7. If none of the repair flows is additive, there is one group per repair flow: a=group:FEC-FR S4 R5, a=group:FEC-FR S4 R6 and a=group:FEC-FR S4 R7.
sections.plainLanguage: One line names one set of related streams. The same stream can be named on two lines, and streams named on the same line can be used together to repair missing data.

sections.title: Grouping When Flows Share One RTP Session
sections.content:
RFC 5576 defines an SDP media-level attribute called ssrc-group for grouping the RTP streams that are SSRC multiplexed and carried in the same RTP session. The grouping is based on the Synchronization Source (SSRC) identifiers. Because SSRC-multiplexed RTP streams are defined in the same m line, the group attribute cannot be used for them.

The semantics of FEC-FR for the ssrc-group attribute are the same as those defined for the group attribute, except that the SSRC identifiers designate the FEC grouping associations: a=ssrc-group:FEC-FR *(SP ssrc-id).

SSRC identifiers for the RTP streams carried in the same RTP session must be unique, but they are not guaranteed to be unique among different RTP sessions, so the ssrc-group attribute must only be used at the media level. Additivity is handled as in Section 4.2: the repair flows included in one a=ssrc-group line must be additive, and repair flows that are not additive must be indicated in separate lines.

In the document's example, one video stream and one audio stream share a session, and only the video is protected: a=ssrc-group:FEC-FR 1000 2110. The document notes that real SSRC values are random 32-bit numbers and may be much larger than the ones shown, and that the receiver cannot know which SSRC identifier is associated with which payload type before it has received a packet for each stream.
sections.plainLanguage: When several streams share one session, the list cannot name them by media line, so each stream is named by its 32-bit identifier instead. The rules about which streams belong together stay the same.

sections.title: The Deprecated FEC Semantics and the Fallback
sections.content:
The original FEC semantics from RFC 4756 are deprecated. Sessions negotiated between two endpoints implementing this document must use FEC-FR and not FEC.

Under the old semantics a source or repair flow can only appear in a single a=group:FEC line, so all the source and repair flows that are somehow related to each other have to be listed in the same line. The Figure 1 scenario would become a=group:FEC S1 S2 R1 R2 regardless of which repair flow protected which source flow, and the Figure 3 scenario would become a=group:FEC S4 R5 R6 R7 regardless of which repair flows were additive. The interpretation of those lines would be ambiguous.

In an offer/answer exchange (RFC 3264), the answerer may not understand line grouping, or may understand it but not the FEC-FR semantics. From the viewpoint of the offerer, these cases are indistinguishable. The answerer responds with an answer that ignores the grouping attribute, or with a refusal such as 488 Not Acceptable Here or 606 Not Acceptable in SIP.

If the offerer supports the old semantics, it must first check whether using them would create any ambiguity. If the old semantics still provide an exact association among the source and repair flows, the offerer should send a new offer using FEC. If an exact association cannot be described, it must send, or should send after a refusal, a new offer without FEC.
sections.plainLanguage: If the other end does not understand the new list format, the sender tries the old format, but only if the old format can still say exactly what it means. If it cannot, the sender offers the session without the repair streams.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The document describes a weak threat: the FEC grouping could be modified to indicate relationships that do not exist, which may result in FEC failing to protect, or mishandling, other media payload streams. The receiver should do an integrity check on the SDP and follow the security considerations of SDP in RFC 4566, trusting only SDP from trusted sources.

For IANA, the document registers FEC, marked Deprecated, and FEC-FR in the registry for the semantics of the group SDP attribute, and FEC-FR in the registry for the semantics of the ssrc-group SDP attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone alters the list, the receiver may use the wrong repair streams. So the receiver should check that the list came from a source it trusts.
